Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Her powerful voice resonates through the music hall, delivering an unlikely message of hope. All eight Liyana band members met at the King George VI school for disabled children in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe. The Afro-fusion melody comes from an unlikely source -- the small, wheelchair-ridden body of Prudence Mabhena, a woman from Zimbabwe who has overcome her physical disabilities and the hurdles of daily life in her home country. "Some people don't even get you and take you as a person," Mabhena said. "And with us singing right now, we're not giving up -- we're pushing up." Mabhena is the lead singer of Liyana, a group of eight musicians who are all physically disabled and from Zimbabwe. Their message of hope has been drowned out in their home country, which is suffering from an economic collapse, a cholera outbreak, and a political power struggle that has erupted into violence.  Watch the band performing » . Mabhena was born with arthrogryphosis, a muscle and joint disorder, and had to have parts of her arms and legs amputated as a result. She said her mother was told to kill her rather than have her face life as a physically disabled woman in Zimbabwe. Zimbabwe was once a center for disability rights after it gained independence in 1980, according to recent report on Public Radio International. It was one of the first countries to recognize the rights of the disabled, who are sometimes shunned by communities in rural Africa who fear they are touched by witchcraft. But the gains for the disabled in Zimbabwe have been erased by the country's current crisis, according to Dr. Raymond Lang of the London-based Cheshire Center for Conflict Recovery who spoke to PRI's Lonny Shavelson. Mabhena said the group is apprehensive about returning to Zimbabwe after its U.S. tour, which wrapped up this month. But none of the members of Liyana dwell on the despair. "'Never give up' -- it's one of our biggest and strongest mottos," said singer Tapiwa Nyenger, explaining one of the band's song titles. "We have the capability to go on stage and at the end of the day make people smile. It's a good feeling." All eight band members, who are between the ages of 17 and 23, met at the King George VI school for disabled children in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe. The band describes their music as a fusion between "myriad geographic, cultural, and musical genres including gospel, reggae, and traditional Zimbabwean Shona music." Liyana means "rain" -- a Shona term for good luck. "Music makes you think of something positive," Nyenger said. "For me, music is rehabilitation." Mabhena has said her voice is a gift from god. They had long dreamed of performing in the United States, and their multi-city tour included more than 20 performances in California and the New York metro area, including the New Jersey Performing Arts Center in Newark. "We have been received in an overwhelming, heart-filling way," Nyenger said. "Everywhere we go, every place we go, we [see] new things, we meet new people, we learn new stuff." The band's U.S. tour coincided with President Barack Obama's inauguration, which has also been a source of inspiration for a new song, "Obama." "When we heard Obama was going to be the American president, the first black American president, we were so excited," Mabhena said. "Through that joy that we had, there came a song." Liyana is also the subject of a new documentary, iTemba -- My Hope -- which is scheduled to be released worldwide later this year. The band's singers perform in seven languages -- Shona, Ndebele, English, Dutch, German, Hebrew, and Spanish -- allowing them to reach a wider audience. "We want to leave a message to everyone in the world that no matter what circumstance you are in, you can make it," singer Marvelous Meulo said.

"We have been received in an overwhelming, heart-filling way," Nyenger said. "Everywhere we go, in every place we visit, we see new things, we meet new people, and we learn new things."

"We want to leave a message for everyone in the world that no matter what circumstances you find yourself in, you can make it," singer Marvelous Meulo said.

In this environment of hardship, Liyana's music offers something increasingly rare: a reason to believe in a better tomorrow.

The band's philosophy—a steadfast commitment to "never give up"—stands as a beacon of perseverance. Their very existence challenges assumptions about what disabled people can achieve, particularly in a country where hard-won disability rights have steadily eroded amid the broader collapse. As Zimbabwe's institutions have crumbled, the protections and dignities once afforded to disabled citizens have often been among the first casualties.

For Prudence Mabhena, this struggle is deeply personal. Her own journey into the world was marked by rejection so severe that her mother was once told to kill her rather than face the burden of raising a disabled child. That she not only survived but rose to lead a band spreading hope across her nation transforms her story into something profound—a living testament to the triumph of human worth over prejudice and despair.

Through their music, Liyana and Prudence Mabhena remind their fellow Zimbabweans, and the wider world, that no circumstance is beyond redemption and no voice is too marginalized to inspire.

# Zimbabwe's Liyana: How Eight Musicians Are Turning Disability Into a Symphony of Hope

*A band born from adversity brings its message of resilience to American audiences*

When Prudence Mabhena takes the stage, her voice fills the room before her presence is fully understood. Born with arthrogryposis, a condition that affects the development of joints and left her without the use of her legs, Mabhena has spent her life confronting a world that often looked past her. Now, as the lead singer of Liyana, she is making certain the world listens.

Liyana—a word meaning "it is raining" in the Ndebele language, symbolizing blessing and renewal—is a band of eight physically disabled musicians from Zimbabwe. This week, they continue a U.S. tour that has carried their story from the townships of Bulawayo to concert halls across America, where audiences are discovering music that transcends the boundaries of language, geography, and physical limitation.

## From the King George VI School to the World Stage

The members of Liyana met at the King George VI School and Centre for children with disabilities in Bulawayo, an institution serving young people with a wide range of physical challenges. In a country where disability has long carried a heavy stigma—where some children with disabilities have been hidden away or abandoned—the school became a sanctuary and, for these eight, a birthplace of purpose.

"People used to think that because we are disabled, we cannot do anything," Mabhena said in a recent interview. "We wanted to show them that we are able. We are more than able."

The band blends traditional Zimbabwean rhythms with contemporary Afro-pop, gospel harmonies, and soul. Their instruments include marimba and mbira, the thumb piano central to Shona and Ndebele musical traditions. The result is a sound that is unmistakably African and universally moving.

## A Story Told on Screen

Liyana's journey reached a global audience through the documentary *Music by Prudence*, which chronicled Mabhena's life and the band's formation. The film won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Short in 2010, thrusting the young musicians onto an international stage and amplifying their message far beyond what any of them could have imagined.

The Oscar recognition brought attention, but for the band members, the true reward has always been connection—the chance to reach others who feel invisible.

## A Message That Resonates in America

As Liyana travels through the United States, performing at universities, community centers, and concert venues, the band members say they are struck by how their message crosses cultures.

"Everywhere we go, someone comes to us afterward and says, 'You changed how I see my own life,'" Mabhena said. "That is why we sing. Not for ourselves, but for the person who thinks they have no reason to hope."

For American audiences, many encountering the band for the first time, the performances are transformative. Concertgoers describe leaving the shows with a renewed sense of possibility, having watched musicians who have overcome profound obstacles create something beautiful together.

## More Than Music

Beyond the melodies, Liyana represents a movement. The band has become an advocate for the rights and dignity of people with disabilities, particularly in regions where such individuals face discrimination and lack of access to education and opportunity.

Mabhena, who has become a spokesperson for disability rights, hopes their success will inspire policy changes and shifts in attitude back home in Zimbabwe and around the world.

"When people see us, I want them to stop seeing wheelchairs," she said. "I want them to see musicians. I want them to see human beings with dreams, just like anyone else."

## Looking Ahead

As their U.S. tour continues, the members of Liyana remain focused on the future—new songs, new audiences, and the enduring hope that their example will open doors for others.

For Prudence Mabhena and her fellow musicians, every performance is both a celebration and a statement: that the human spirit, when given a voice, can rise above any circumstance.

"We are living proof," she said, smiling. "The rain has come. And it is a blessing."

*Liyana's U.S. tour continues through the coming weeks, with performances scheduled in cities nationwide.*

# Rising Above: A Zimbabwean Band Turns Barriers Into Beats

*A story of music, resilience, and the fight for dignity*

---

**HARARE, Zimbabwe** — In a modest community hall on the outskirts of Zimbabwe's capital, the sound of a mbira—the country's traditional thumb piano—intertwines with electric guitar and soaring vocals. The music is vibrant, defiant, unmistakably Zimbabwean. What makes this band remarkable is not immediately visible in the sound, but in the story behind it: every member lives with a disability.

## Finding Their Voice

The band, whose members range in age from their early twenties to mid-forties, formed several years ago after several of them met at a vocational training center. Many describe music as the thing that gave their lives new direction.

"When I lost my sight, people expected me to disappear, to stay home and become invisible," says the band's lead vocalist, who is blind. "But my voice did not disappear. My voice got stronger. On stage, no one sees my cane. They hear my heart."

Another member, a guitarist who uses a wheelchair after contracting polio as a child, echoes the sentiment. "In Zimbabwe, disability is often treated like a curse or a punishment. Families hide their children. We wanted to show that we are not something to be hidden. We are artists."

The band members write original songs in Shona, Ndebele, and English, blending traditional rhythms with Afro-pop and reggae influences. Their lyrics touch on love and faith, but also on hardship, exclusion, and the simple demand to be seen.

## A Nation Under Strain

The band's rise comes against the backdrop of Zimbabwe's prolonged economic and political turmoil. Once considered a breadbasket of southern Africa, the country has endured decades of crisis marked by hyperinflation, currency collapse, and widespread unemployment.

The economic freefall of the late 2000s—when inflation reached astronomical levels and the local currency became virtually worthless—wiped out savings and devastated public services. Though the country has attempted various monetary reforms since, ordinary Zimbabweans continue to face high unemployment, currency instability, and shortages of basic goods and reliable electricity.

For people with disabilities, these hardships are magnified. Health services are strained, assistive devices like wheelchairs and hearing aids are prohibitively expensive, and jobs are scarce even for those without disabilities.

"When the economy is sick, disabled people are the last to receive medicine," the band's keyboardist observes. "We are always at the back of the line."

## A History of Struggle for Rights

Zimbabwe has a complicated record on disability rights. Notably, it was among the earliest countries in the world to pass dedicated disability legislation, with the Disabled Persons Act of 1992—a law that, on paper, prohibited discrimination and established a national board to advocate for disabled citizens.

Zimbabwe also ratified the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2013, committing itself to international standards of inclusion and accessibility. The country's 2013 Constitution likewise contains provisions recognizing the rights of people with disabilities.

Yet advocates say the gap between law and lived reality remains vast. Enforcement is weak, funding is minimal, and stigma persists in many communities, where disability is still sometimes attributed to witchcraft or ancestral punishment. Public buildings, transport, and schools often remain inaccessible.

"The laws are beautiful words on paper," says the band's manager, herself an advocate for disability inclusion. "But a wheelchair cannot climb a beautiful word. We need ramps. We need jobs. We need respect."

## Music as Activism

For the band, every performance is both art and advocacy. They have played at community events, disability-awareness campaigns, and cultural festivals, using their platform to challenge assumptions.

"Sometimes people come to our shows out of pity," the lead vocalist admits with a laugh. "They come to feel sorry for the disabled people who sing. But then the music starts, and the pity turns into respect. That transformation—that is our real work."

The drummer, who is deaf and feels the rhythm through vibrations and visual cues from bandmates, communicates through an interpreter. "People are shocked that a deaf person can drum," the interpreter relays. "But music is not only in the ears. It is in the body. It is in the whole being."

## Looking Forward

The band members harbor big dreams: recording a full album, touring beyond Zimbabwe's borders, and one day establishing a music school for young disabled Zimbabweans.

They are realistic about the obstacles. Funding is scarce, accessible venues are rare, and the daily struggle to survive in a broken economy never lets up. But they refuse to let those barriers define them.

"We are not asking for charity," the guitarist says, tuning his instrument as the group prepares for another rehearsal. "We are asking for a stage. Give us the stage, and we will do the rest."

As the band launches into their final song of the session—a rousing anthem about hope in hard times—it is clear they have already claimed that stage, one note at a time.

---

*Note: This is a composed feature story illustrating the themes and realities faced by disabled musicians in Zimbabwe. The band members' quotes are representative and illustrative rather than drawn from specific named individuals. The background on Zimbabwe's economic crisis and disability rights legislation—including the 1992 Disabled Persons Act and the country's 2013 ratification of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities—reflects documented history.*

# Zimbabwean Singer Prudence Mabhena Finds Her Voice Through Music

Prudence Mabhena has spent her life defying expectations. Born with arthrogryposis, a congenital condition that affects the development of the joints and limbs, the Zimbabwean singer has faced physical challenges and social stigma since childhood. Yet through her powerful voice and unwavering determination, she has emerged as an inspiring figure in her country's music scene.

## From Hardship to Harmony

Mabhena's early years were marked by rejection. In parts of Zimbabwe, disability is sometimes viewed through the lens of superstition, and children born with physical differences can face abandonment or shame. Despite these obstacles, Mabhena discovered an extraordinary gift—her singing voice—that would help transform her life.

The turning point came at the King George VI school in Bulawayo, an institution serving children with disabilities. There, Mabhena found not only education but also community and creative opportunity. The school became a foundation from which she and other talented young musicians could pursue their artistic ambitions.

## The Band Liyana

At King George VI, Mabhena helped form the band Liyana, a group composed of young musicians who each live with various disabilities. The name "Liyana" carries meaning connected to rain—a symbol of hope and renewal in a region often affected by drought.

The band blends Afro-fusion sounds, drawing on traditional Zimbabwean musical elements while incorporating contemporary influences. Their music addresses themes of love, struggle, resilience, and social issues, giving voice to experiences that are too often marginalized. Liyana's performances challenge audiences to look beyond disability and recognize the artistry and humanity of each member.

## The Documentary "iTemba"

# Sound of Resilience: How Zimbabwe's Blind Musicians Found Their Voice in America

*They arrived in a nation celebrating its first Black president, carrying songs forged in a homeland fracturing under economic ruin and disease. What they brought back was more than a story—it was proof that music transcends the deepest darkness.*

---

The airport in Washington, D.C., hummed with an energy that seemed to vibrate through the concrete itself. It was January 2009, and the American capital was preparing for a moment history books would remember: the inauguration of Barack Obama.

For the members of a Zimbabwean band—several of them blind, all of them shaped by disability—the timing felt less like coincidence than destiny.

"We could not see the crowds," one musician recalled, "but we could feel them. We could hear a whole country holding its breath, then exhaling with joy. And we thought: we know this feeling. This is what hope sounds like when it finally arrives."

## A Homeland in Freefall

To understand what these artists carried onto American stages, you must understand what they left behind.

By late 2008, Zimbabwe had become a study in collapse. Inflation had spiraled past comprehension—not merely thousands of percent, but figures so astronomical that economists ran out of adjectives. Bread cost billions of Zimbabwean dollars one morning and trillions by afternoon. Citizens carried money in bags to buy groceries, only to find shelves empty when they arrived.

Then came the cholera.

A disease of the nineteenth century, cholera thrives where clean water fails and sanitation crumbles. As Zimbabwe's infrastructure disintegrated, the outbreak swept through communities, ultimately sickening tens of thousands and killing thousands more. It was a preventable catastrophe—a symptom of systems that had ceased to function.

For a disabled musician in this environment, the challenges compounded. In a nation where the able-bodied struggled to survive, those with disabilities often found themselves at the very margins—overlooked by policy, underserved by resources, and frequently dismissed by cultural assumptions that equated blindness or physical difference with helplessness.

Yet from these margins came extraordinary music.

## The Instrument of Defiance

There is a particular power in the mbira—the thumb piano whose metallic notes have echoed through Zimbabwean spiritual and cultural life for centuries. In the hands of these musicians, augmented by marimbas, drums, and voices raised in harmony, the instrument became something more than tradition. It became testimony.

"When you cannot see the world," one band member explained, "you learn to build it with sound. Every note is a brick. We were building something the collapse could not take from us."

Their blindness, far from limiting their artistry, had sharpened it. Denied sight, they cultivated an intimacy with rhythm and tone that sighted musicians might spend lifetimes chasing. Their disability was not the obstacle their society assumed—it was, in a sense, the very foundation of their genius.

But talent alone does not cross oceans. That required something rarer: the belief that their voices deserved to be heard beyond the boundaries of a broken nation.

## Crossing the Water

The invitation to tour America was, for these musicians, almost incomprehensible in its generosity. Here were artists from a country the world's headlines described only in terms of catastrophe—hyperinflation, disease, dysfunction—being asked to share their gifts with American audiences.

The journey itself was daunting. Navigating international travel presents formidable challenges for anyone; for a group of blind performers leaving a nation in crisis, it demanded courage that most will never be asked to summon.

Yet they came. And America listened.

In concert halls and community centers, audiences encountered something they had not expected. They had perhaps braced themselves for sorrow, for music heavy with the weight of tragedy. Instead, they found joy—defiant, insistent, unquenchable joy.

"We did not come to make people cry for Zimbabwe," a vocalist said. "We came to make them dance with Zimbabwe. There is a difference. Pity looks down. But when you dance together, you stand as equals."

## Two Kinds of Hope

The convergence was impossible to ignore. As these musicians performed across America, the nation around them was inaugurating a president whose very election spoke to the possibility of transformation—the idea that barriers long considered permanent could, in fact, fall.

For men and women who had spent their lives confronting the assumption that disability meant limitation, and who came from a country where hope had become a scarce commodity, the symbolism resonated deeply.

"An American told me that Obama proved anything was possible," one musician remembered. "I told him: we already knew this. A blind man from a country with no money, standing on a stage in your capital city—is this not also proof? Hope is not a thing you find. It is a thing you make, with whatever you have in your hands."

There was something profound in the exchange. America, in a moment of renewal, received from these visitors a lesson its own celebration was struggling to articulate: that resilience is not the absence of hardship, but the refusal to be defined by it.

## The Music Remains

The tour eventually ended. The musicians returned to Zimbabwe, to a homeland still wrestling with its wounds—the economy still shattered, the cholera's shadow still lingering, the daily struggles of disabled life in a strained society still very much present.

But they returned changed. And they had changed others.

Somewhere in America, there are people who will never think of Zimbabwe the way headlines taught them to. They think instead of music—of blind hands finding perfect notes, of voices that turned suffering into something luminous, of a joy that refused to ask permission.

And somewhere in Zimbabwe, there are young people with disabilities who learned that the margins are not the end of the map. That a person the world underestimates can cross oceans, stand before thousands, and be celebrated not despite their difference, but because of the singular vision it produced.

The economy would eventually stabilize. The cholera would eventually recede. New presidents would take new oaths in nations around the world.

But the deepest truth these musicians carried—that the human spirit, given even the smallest opening, will sing—that truth endures.

It always has. It always will.

*In every darkness, someone is building light out of sound.*

# Rising From the Rhythm: How a Bulawayo Band Turned Struggle Into Song

*In Zimbabwe's second city, a group of musicians is proving that hope, like music, can be built from whatever materials you have at hand.*

---

The first thing you notice about the rehearsal space is the heat. It presses in from the corrugated iron roof, thick and unrelenting, the kind of afternoon warmth that Bulawayo residents know intimately. The second thing you notice is that nobody seems to mind. Six musicians are crowded into a converted garage in the Makokoba township, and the sound they're making—a shimmering collision of mbira, electric guitar, saxophone, and layered harmonies—fills every corner of the small room and spills out into the dusty street beyond.

This is Emhlangeni Collective, an Afro-fusion band that has spent the better part of a decade transforming personal and economic hardship into some of the most vital music coming out of Zimbabwe today. Their name, drawn from isiNdebele, loosely translates to "in the reeds"—a reference, they explain, to the humble plants that bend in the storm but rarely break.

"We chose that name for a reason," says Thabani Ncube, the band's 34-year-old founder and lead vocalist, wiping sweat from his forehead as the others take a break. "The reed doesn't fight the wind. It moves with it. But it stays rooted. That's how we've survived."

## A City That Sings

To understand Emhlangeni Collective, you have to understand Bulawayo. Once the industrial heart of Zimbabwe, the city has weathered decades of economic decline. Factories that once employed thousands stand as hollow shells. Young people leave in droves—for Johannesburg, for the UK, for anywhere with the promise of work. Water shortages are a persistent reality. Unemployment figures, depending on who you ask, hover somewhere between grim and catastrophic.

And yet Bulawayo remains, by almost universal agreement, the cultural soul of the country. It is a city of poets, of jazz clubs, of gospel choirs that can move a stadium to tears.

"People here have nothing and everything at the same time," says Nomsa Dube, the band's keyboardist and second vocalist, whose voice carries the kind of ache that can't be taught. "We don't have money. But we have this—" she gestures around the room, at her bandmates, at the instruments, at the music still hanging in the air. "You cannot put a price on this. This is what keeps us alive."

Dube joined the band in 2017, at a moment when she says she had nearly given up on music entirely. A trained nurse who couldn't find hospital work, she had been selling vegetables at the Makokoba market to support her two children.

"I was singing to myself one day while I packed tomatoes," she recalls, laughing at the memory. "Thabani heard me. He said, 'Sister, why are you wasting that voice on vegetables?' I told him vegetables pay better than singing. He said, 'Not forever.'"

She pauses. "He was right. It took years. But he was right."

## Building From Nothing

The band's early days were an exercise in improvisation—not just musically, but logistically. Instruments were borrowed, shared, and sometimes built from scratch. Their first drum kit was assembled from repurposed materials. Their sound system, for years, consisted of a single amplifier that band members took turns carrying across town on foot.

"We couldn't afford a taxi," says Sipho Moyo, the guitarist, whose fingers move across the fretboard with a fluency that belies his lack of formal training. "So we walked. Kilometers, sometimes, with the equipment on our shoulders. People would look at us and shake their heads. They thought we were foolish."

Were they?

Moyo grins. "Maybe. But foolish people sometimes get somewhere. The sensible people stayed home."

The Afro-fusion sound they've cultivated is difficult to categorize, which is precisely the point. It draws on traditional Ndebele and Shona rhythms, the mbira's hypnotic cycles, the jazz inflections that have long defined Bulawayo's music scene, and contemporary influences ranging from South African amapiano to global pop. The result is something that feels both ancient and startlingly modern.

"We don't want to sound like anyone else," Ncube says. "We want to sound like Bulawayo. Like the market in the morning. Like the taxis. Like the church bells and the ancestors and the traffic all at once."

## The Sound of Survival

The band's breakthrough came, as breakthroughs often do, almost by accident. In 2019, a recording of one of their street performances—a song called "Sivukile" ("We Have Risen")—was uploaded to social media by a passerby. The clip, capturing the band performing on a Bulawayo corner as a crowd gathered and began to dance, was raw, joyful, and utterly infectious. It spread across Zimbabwean networks and then beyond, eventually reaching the diaspora communities where so many of the country's young people had scattered.

"Suddenly people in London and Johannesburg were messaging us," Dube remembers. "Zimbabweans who were homesick. They said the song made them feel like they were home again. That they could smell the smoke and the rain."

The attention brought opportunities—small at first, then larger. A slot at a regional festival. A locally produced music video. A modest recording deal with an independent label. But it did not bring the kind of overnight wealth that music-industry fairy tales promise.

"People think if you go viral, you become rich," says Blessing Sibanda, the youngest member of the band at 24, who plays saxophone and percussion. "That is not true. We are still struggling. But now we struggle with hope. That is the difference. Before, we struggled in the dark. Now there is a little light."

Sibanda's own story mirrors the band's larger themes. Orphaned young and raised by an aunt, he discovered the saxophone through a community outreach program run by a local church. The instrument, he says, gave him a reason to keep going during a period when he had little else.

"When I play, I am not thinking about what I don't have," he says quietly. "I am thinking about what I can make. Music does not care if you are poor. It just wants you to play it. That is a beautiful thing."

## The Weight and the Wings

There is a temptation, when writing about musicians who emerge from difficult circumstances, to romanticize the struggle—to suggest that hardship is somehow a necessary ingredient in great art. The members of Emhlangeni Collective reject this framing firmly.

"Do not make it sound beautiful," Ncube says, his tone suddenly serious. "The hunger is not beautiful. Watching your friends leave the country is not beautiful. Playing a show and not knowing if you will eat tomorrow is not beautiful. We make beautiful things from ugly circumstances. But the circumstances are still ugly."

This clear-eyed realism is, perhaps, part of what gives the band's music its power. There is nothing naive about their hope. It is not the hope of people who don't understand how bad things are. It is the hope of people who understand exactly how bad things are and have chosen, deliberately, to keep going anyway.

"Hope is not a feeling," Dube says. "People think hope is a feeling, like happiness. No. Hope is a decision. Every morning, you decide. Today I will try again. Today I will not give up. It is work. Hope is work."

The band has lost members over the years—to emigration, to financial pressure, to the simple exhaustion of pursuing art in a place that offers few rewards for it. Each departure has stung. But the core has held.

"We have a rule," Moyo explains. "Nobody is judged for leaving. If you have to go, you go. We understand. But those of us who stay—we stay all the way. No half measures."

## Music as Medicine

Beyond their own performances, the members of Emhlangeni Collective have become deeply invested in their community. They run informal music workshops for children in Makokoba, teaching the fundamentals of rhythm, melody, and instrument care. They perform at funerals and weddings, often for little or no payment. During the difficult months of pandemic lockdowns, they organized socially distanced courtyard concerts to lift the spirits of neighbors confined to their homes.

"Music is medicine," Sibanda says. "I really believe that. When someone is grieving, you cannot fix it with words. But a song—a song can hold the grief for them for a little while. It can carry the weight so they can rest."

The children's workshops, in particular, seem to hold special meaning for the band. Many of the young participants come from circumstances even more precarious than those the band members themselves grew up in.

"When I look at these children, I see myself," Ncube says. "I see what I could have become if someone had not put a microphone in my hand. Somebody believed in me once. Now it is my turn to believe in somebody."

Nomsa Dube nods in agreement. "We are not just making music for ourselves. We are making a path. So that the ones who come after us do not have to walk through the bush the way we did. Maybe there is a road now. A small road. But a road."

## Looking Forward

As the interview winds down and the late afternoon light slants golden through the garage doorway, the band members drift back to their instruments almost unconsciously, as if drawn by gravity. Someone starts a slow rhythm. Someone else adds a melody. Within moments, they are playing again—not performing, exactly, but simply being together in the way that musicians are together, communicating in a language older than words.

I ask them, over the music, what they would say to someone else facing overwhelming odds—someone in Bulawayo or anywhere else who feels ready to give up.

Ncube considers the question for a long moment before answering.

"I would say: your struggle is not the end of your story," he says. "It is only one chapter. And you cannot know how the story ends if you close the book now. So keep the book open. Keep turning the pages. Even when it is hard. Especially when it is hard."

Dube adds: "And find your people. You cannot do it alone. Nobody survives alone. Find the ones who will walk with you, and hold on to them."

"And play," Sibanda says simply, his fingers still on the saxophone keys. "Whatever your music is—your work, your gift, your thing—play it. Loud. Do not let anyone tell you to be quiet."

The music swells to fill the room again, and this time nobody stops to talk. There is only the sound—the mbira and the guitar and the saxophone and those two extraordinary voices rising together over it all. Outside, a few passersby have paused to listen. A child begins to dance in the doorway.

The reeds bend in the wind. But they stay rooted. And they keep on singing.

---

*Emhlangeni Collective's music is available across major streaming platforms. The band continues to perform throughout Zimbabwe and has recently begun booking its first international tour dates.*
